output.headline: US and China extend Busan trade truce to January as Trump gives Xi rare welcome to Washington
output.standfirst:
Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said the ‘Busan agreement’ truce would run until 10 January, as Trump personally welcomed Xi at Joint Base Andrews with a red carpet and military flyover.

  • AI, trade, Taiwan and climate: what will and won’t be on agenda at Trump-Xi summit
output.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump personally welcomed Xi Jinping to the US, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to open his state visit to Washington.

US service members lined a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet for the lavish ceremony that greeted Xi’s plane, which also included a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries.

Trump and the first lady, Melania, travelled to the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, on Wednesday evening to personally shake hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan – a departure from the usual practice of presidents welcoming foreign leaders at the White House.

Related: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China

World leaders are gathering in New York for the United Nations general assembly at the same time as Xi’s visit, though the Chinese leader will not address the meeting – he has attended the UNGA only once since becoming president in 2012.

Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters: “It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is ⁠coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York. I think a lot of people will say: ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’”

The US and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan agreement, a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced.

Bessent, who met the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would run until 10 January, two months beyond its original expiry.

A formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives are among the events still to come in the pageantry surrounding the visit.

During the two-day visit, Trump and Xi must also confront a number of thorny issues, including the race in artificial intelligence development, geopolitical instability and the simmering trade war.

Executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and other major tech companies have been invited by the White House to a state dinner being held for Xi on Thursday.

The one unscripted moment in the carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony came when a US military jet flew overhead as Trump and Xi stood on the red carpet listening to the US national anthem: video of the moment showed Xi remaining impassive, as did the wives of both men, while Trump visibly winced and recoiled at the sound of the flyover.

Widely mocked online, the moment was captured on a White House livestream, though it was not included in the edited highlights of the ceremony that Trump’s aides released later.

The US and China have long been competing on technology in general, but the race to advance AI in particular has become a major topic among tech companies, especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.

Trump has promoted more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race, having dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people.

Trump wrote on Truth Social last week: “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,”

The president and members of his administration have argued that leading in AI also means leading the world militarily and economically, raising the stakes further for both the US and China.

The ceremonial displays expected throughout Xi’s visit reciprocate the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.

By choosing to greet the Chinese leader at his plane rather than at the White House, Trump signalled how far he is willing to go to honour Xi.

“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit, speaking to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”

Robert Mackey contributed reporting
